claims.text: Combined in-situ HT-XRD and TGA can reliably characterize oxidation kinetics and phase evolution in metallic alloys under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
A polished, homogenized metal or alloy, such as a Ni-based superalloy, is an appropriate initial state for the proposed characterization.
TGA measurements can track mass changes during oxidation.
In-situ HT-XRD can track phase transformations during oxidation.
Exposure at 800–1100°C in air or controlled oxygen flow can be used to study high-temperature oxidation.
High-temperature oxidizing exposure leads to development and transformation of an oxide scale on the alloy surface.
At high temperatures in an oxygen-rich environment, an alloy undergoes oxidation.
High-temperature oxidation may produce multiple oxide phases.
TGA detects mass gain caused by oxide growth.
HT-XRD identifies the crystallographic structures and evolution of oxide phases.
TGA mass gains correspond to the growth rate of oxide layers.
Changes in HT-XRD patterns indicate oxide nucleation, growth, and transformation.
Without combined in-situ HT-XRD and TGA, oxidation-induced mass and phase changes would be less precisely correlated.
Less precise correlation of mass and phase changes can provide incomplete information about high-temperature material degradation.
Oxidation behavior can differ with oxygen partial pressure or gas composition.
Oxidation rates and phase evolution depend on alloy composition, temperature, and atmosphere.
SEM can provide additional post-exposure confirmation of oxide microstructure.
A lack of correspondence between TGA mass changes and new HT-XRD peaks would show that the joint method is insufficient or inaccurate for detecting oxidation and phase transitions.
